blocks.x: Donnell Howard, April 21st, 1957, Real 1.
Now this is Donnell Howard. Oh, goodness. I just want to make sure that I remember your distinguished voice. Donnell Howard, how old are you? About 74 now?
No, I was 50 last July. Really? Yeah. Where were you born? Born in Chicago, 1906. It's July 25th.
Because he was born the same year. Uh-huh. That's what he told me.

Well, I don't know. That's what he told me. He kept saying one time, when we went to school, this is me, I don't say that, I don't know what I said. I mean, where did he get that we stuff? When we went to school, I don't know what he meant.
Is 6 years older than you?
6 years older than you. How many? I haven't any idea. He's older than I am, no? He is?
Were you born right in Chicago?
Who, Muggsy? No, you. Sure. 3528 Federal. It was a treat.
Oh, yeah?
This is two blocks from Army Institute. Yeah. You all know the school of technology now.
When did you first learn music?
I mean, playing or lessons? Lessons. Only. I was 7 years old.
And what were you studying?
Violin.
Violin. Was it a private teacher or at school?
Yeah. I studied under a teacher that gave my father some lessons.
Was your father a musician?
Yeah.
What did you play?
Violin. Cornel and piano. Where? In Chicago.
With what kind of...
Oh, he played in night spots. When he became ill, he was working at a place called Pony Morris, 21st and Warbash.
He was a dance man musician, then. Thank you, sir.
Thanks. Well, I don't know about the dance band. It wasn't so... A little different than night life, then. More singing and feature numbers, you know? You know how much dance music?
Cut for a minute and...
All right. Let's stop for two minutes. I know that. Did you know that that was a great photographer?

Well, I heard about it. What? Yeah, somebody said that you were taking a lot of pictures in New York. I asked about you one time. It was Bob Scobie, I think, when New Yorker, Turk 1. Saw you around here taking a whole lot of pictures. Oh, that and there's your head again. He's a first-rate photographer.
There's no one who's known as Weegee around town.
Did you have to walk in there just to have a picture? Yeah, that big knee you see come into the picture.
Mr. Howard, sir, you were saying that you took your first lessons when you were seven years old on violin. Uh-huh. And that your father was a professional musician.
Yeah.
What kind of music did your father play?
All types, just like I did. All types? Yes, sir.
So how long did you study?
Oh, until I made my first runaway from home.
Well, tell us about that.
14 years old.
By the way, were you studying at school or with a private teacher?
No, no. I was a violin teacher. His name was Toad Johnson. Old man had whiskies. Yes, sir, what are you doing? Hey, is that thing insured?
Huh? I'll send you a picture. You'll find out.
No, you tell them in a few minutes, but they're going to tear all the pieces. Huh, huh, huh, huh.
So why did you run away from home now? Tell us about that.

Went to work with him. See, they wouldn't let me work. Oh, you remember Clarence Jones? Yes. He put me in the union when I was 12 years old. I worked at a theater in Chicago, a panorama theater. There was four of us, violin, cornet, piano, drums. Schoolbird found out about it and made me quit on account of child labor law. Wouldn't let me work, no kidding.
What kind of place were you working at?
A theater. Pit. Oh, pit. Yeah.
Four-piece band.
That's right.
What did you play?
Violin. What kind of tunes? Regular movie picture music. You were? No sound. Were you reading? Read it? Yes, certainly.
Were you a good sight reader by this age, at 12?
Well, yes, certainly.
Certainly. In those, you had really a very thorough academic training, huh?

I did. Made my first debut in Alderwood Baptist Church when I was nine years old. My mother played the piano. And you played violin? Scared the dead, knees, felt like they were shaking. Why? That's all I. I remember forgetting when the boy played on before I leaned over to the piano.
I said, Mama, can you see my knees shaking?

I said, no. It felt like it was doing like that. Yeah, it was funny. Yeah. This band, you see, they introduced me to running from home. Because I couldn't work here, nobody did know me in Milwaukee. And it was the first long pantsuit I ever had in my life. We got off the train and they waited for the pawn shop to open. Went in there and bought me a long, a first long pantsuit. It was a tuxedo. I can't stand them today. Yeah. Well, you went to Milwaukee. At Slick's Palm Garden. With his band. John Wheeler's Ginger Band. You were 12? So that was. No, I was 14 then. That'd be 1920. I was 12 years old. I was 12, not all. 18. 1918. 1918. Great. Nice. They had a sign up. John Wheeler's Jazz Band. Great name of the red letters. J-A-S-S-E. And so they made them take the sign down, see. And they finally replaced it with John Wheeler's Ginger Band. No kidding.
Oh, yeah?
Yeah.
You mean the word jazz had a bad comment.

It looked like they had A-S-S on there instead of Chris, it should have been A-Z-Z, you know. Yeah. But the man didn't want it up there no kind of way since they hadn't made that first mistake, you know. That's crazy. So where'd you go when you ran away from home? Milwaukee. For how long? Well, we played at the Slick's Palm Garden for nine months and went from there to Minneapolis.
What did your folks think about this?

Well, my mother knew where I was first week. I wanted to write and they wouldn't let me. So when I got my first pay, they didn't take nothing out, see. Make a big impression, send a full week's salary home. And my mother was up there that afternoon. Milwaukee was only 85 miles and so on. Yes, yeah. And they talked to her. See, there was two men in that band that worked with my father. And they got in the room and talked to her.
Oh, I see. They used to know you folks.
Yeah. Yeah. See, my mother didn't entertain. What did they do? Hmm? What did they do? Sang and dance. Sang and dance. Sure. They've been out here in the Pantages town. One of those James sisters.
James sisters?
Mm-hmm.
Were they in vaudeville, you mean? To China. They played the circuits and so on.
And then my mother and I was with Rosamund Johnson.
Oh, yeah?
Yeah. What did that show?
Shufar Redman and Redman. You were from a family of musicians and entertainers. That's right. Grandfather and grandmother. So what happens after Milwaukee?
Uh, Minneapolis at Tuchman's Grumor Cafe. German restaurant.
How many pieces was this man?
Eight. I got a picture somewhere.
I sure would like to see it.
Listen, I'd let you have the picture. If you promise you'd give it back to him. Oh, absolutely. That's the only picture I have.
Absolutely. Don't.
Honestly.
Guaranteed 100%. You'll get it back. And right away.
Well, I'll have to send it to you if you don't find it this afternoon.
Yeah, Bob will give you his address at life. All right. You can send it to him and he'll send it right back to you. Okay.

I'd just like to see it. That's the only picture. Just to see what it looks like and what, how you address it. Let's call all the individual names. No, we're in tuxedas. Mm-hmm. Call all the individual names. Here's what it is. It's a big picture in the center.
Mm-hmm.

And then each. You got that too? Right, this way. Yeah. Yeah. You know, I got the pictures around. Yeah. And that's, that was taken from a picture that used to have on, as a, what you call a lobby. Uh-huh. Out in front, that was in front of the place. It's on the easel. What was the first jazz you heard that you remember? About the first jazz I heard I was playing, I guess, myself. Really. Well, how'd you pick it up? Well, I started at that playing. That does, I started after playing. Playing violin solos. Give a concert a couple times. Uh-huh. Right. That was no good for my line of work. Uh. We played, uh, I've been in bands that play all type music, you know.
Well, you sort of picked it up while you were playing, then.
Oh, yeah. When you went with this eight-piece band, what kind of music did you play? What were the tunes you played?
Well, one, one number we used to get a lot of money on was Back Home in Tennessee. I'll never forget that. I don't even know how it'd go.
You don't remember the melody?
No. You had picked me to sing on this thing.
Sure. I mean, just for me, I wouldn't know what the melody is.
Can't help it was for Queen of Sheba. No. But, no, I actually don't remember how it goes. I remember the title. Back Home in Tennessee. Yeah. Guys, we made a lot of money on that.
Did you play stock arrangements or what?
Played, uh, in that band, yes. Stocks. Well, nothing but stocks in that band. Uh-huh. Rap violin, cornet, trombone, saxophone, piano, bass, and drums.
What was the name of the band?
John Wycliffe. John Wycliffe. Nesley, is this a court scene? Am I in court? He's the third time he's asked me that. I'm... Don't be... That is.
Get used to that because I'm going to ask you many more. For the same band? I'm the judge, man. Yeah.
Where were you on the night of October 2nd, 1908? That's right. Now, where were you?
Turkish Army.
He wasn't that old. So that would be about 1918, wasn't it? It was 1918. Yeah. So what did you do?
Did you come back to Chicago? Well, after Minneapolis, we came back to a place called Lamb's Cafe.
Lamb's Cafe?
Yeah, in Milwaukee, in the Randolph Hotel. It was right next door, it slips.
All these places were for white people.
Is that right? That's right. And from there, I left and joined Charles Elgar's band in Chicago. I finally got home sick.
Charles Elgar. How old were you when you joined Elgar?

Two, three... 20 years old. 20 years old. Three years later. No! I don't remember thinking. I'm thinking about 18, 1920. That was 1920. 1920, you were 14 years old. 16 years old. Or 14. And I worked with him for a while.
Now, he was a rather famous band in Chicago, wasn't he? Charles Elgar, yeah. It was a very well-established band.
That's right.
What kind of jobs did Charles Elgar play?

Well, we played the Dreamland Ballroom. That's like the Aragon Ballroom in Trinon is now in Chicago. Or, well, it would be like the... Where was the place Fletcher played until lunch in New York? I played there with him two nights.
The arcade?
No, no. Roseland. That's it. One of those things.
Like the Roseland. Uh-huh. Big ballroom.
That's right. For white people. That's right.
This is not the same dude band where King Oliver plays.

No. No. That's on the south side. Yeah. Well, see? Now, I'm glad you brought that up. I came out there with my band. Get this, my band. You hear this? Yes. I think I told you this before. Tell me again. And when King Oliver finishes and goes down to the Pekin, I come out there with my band with a trumpet. Me.
Really?

Yeah. I didn't tell you that? Oh, yeah. You were playing trumpet? Yeah. Playing the same time music. Drew Otto was playing. Let's see. Who can tell you that? Eddie Garland can tell you. Mine ought to remember that, too. No, I don't know mine. I think it helps. Who'd you have in that band?
Thank God. You were here. You were dressed again. You had two jobs. You played with Elgar and then...
Got off at quarter of 12. You left Elgar at quarter of 12? Uh-huh. Went home and chained my clothes and started this job at 1.30, and Joe Oliver started his job at 1.30.
I did quite... I didn't get that straight.
What's that?
When you went to Pekin to play, you mean Oliver was playing there at the same time?
Oliver played at Dreamland from 8.30 to 1. Yes. And I was playing with Charles Everett from quarter after 8 to quarter of 12 at Greenland. It was on the northwest side of Chicago.
Yes, and then?
And then I went straight home and changed my clothes and come back and went to work at 1.30. I had the band. I was playing, you know, cornet. There wasn't no trumpets there.

Yeah. And was Oliver also playing there? No, he went to the Pekin. And where did you go? At Dreamland. Oh, you went to the Dreamland where Oliver had left. That's how much nerve I had. I didn't... You were following Oliver on the bandstand, you know.

Let's do that now. That's true. I should have had some nerve. I think about that quite a bit. You didn't get to play much jazz with Charlie Elgar, did you? That's all he was playing other than waltzes, playing dance music. Uh-huh. Oh, yeah.
What kind of a place was the Dreamland Ballroom?
Well, it held... It could hold almost 1,000 people. Uh-huh. It was big.
Very fine. What kind of a bandstand? The bandstand.
Well, our bandstand was in the middle. And a cousin of Petrillo's named Cavallo had a band under a band shell right across from us. And we alternated. You alternated? Uh-huh.
Only white people in the audience?

That's all. This was the Dreamland Ballroom? Patty Harmon's Dreamland. That's the man built the Chicago Stadium. What's his name? Patty Harmon. Uh-huh. That's not the Dreamland on the South Side. No. On the North Side.
Was there much... Are you living in Charlie Elgar's bands?

Oh, yeah. Well, they had arrangements, you know, and things like that. And the guy took a solo. He just took a solo. You know who was in that band? You've heard of Cliff King, the Clannett player, haven't you? Yeah. And Buster Bailey. Yeah. They had another fellow from New Orleans named Lane. I don't remember his first name. His name was Lane. Uh-huh. He's a cigar maker, and he played Clannett in the band, too. But when Charlie's band busted up, he didn't play anymore.
How many pieces in Charlie Elgar's band?

Well, we had at that time... 22. 22 pieces. Yeah. Patty Harmon kept the band intact, because when we'd go to the pier anyhow, we'd play the plan, park plan dances, out of the Municipal Pier, which is a Navy pier now. Every Memorial Day, which was Decoration Day, we'd go out to the pier. They'd open up, and they'd stay open until Labor Day.
How much money were you making with that band?
Making... 78-something. Six nights a week. Down at Dreamland, getting $56 a week.
You were rich.
No, I wasn't rich. I was making some money. There's much more than you can make now.
Well, how did you happen to play cornet?
Well, in the Army, I found I could play a bugle.
Were you in the Army?
Yeah. I found I could play a bugle. And I learned I'd play a trumpet at the Army.
How long did you stay in the Army?

I didn't go nowhere. How long were you in the Army? Well, I was in there the whole length of time, but... My uncle's the one that saved me. See, I went in there underage. Uh-huh. Put my age up. See, the 8th Redmond Band at that time was touring different places, and I wanted to go with them, you know, put my age up. I went in there as a drummer. I'm swinging the drum on my knee. Well, how'd you learn all these instruments? Well, I don't know. I don't know how to do it. Ain't the one thing I can give a comment for, and that's a fiddle. I took lessons, really took lessons on a fiddle. Let's pick them up. Pick the others up. Find how I could do it, just kept doing it, I guess. You know why I double on clarinet, don't you?
No.
You never heard the story of that? Nezzy, if you say... I heard it, but that tape didn't hear it. Say, you know, big fibber.
What happened?

Well, I had a... This particular night, I went up to the deluxe where Sidney Baixier was playing, and he's got one of these B-flat curved modern saxophone sopranos. Yes. Playing the hell out of him, no kidding. And I went back raving that next night on the job, so I got Buster Clippet King, and my fibbers come up there to hear him play the saxophone, and he don't pick it up to him. So I went up to the stand and said, Sidney, where's your saxophone? He said, it's in pawn. I said, oh, man. I said, look, you guys up here to hear you. He said, I saved the ticket for $5, and I bought the ticket.
He said, that's all right. Yeah, that's no kidding.

I said, I don't know why, but it did. I had a good boss, because I was squeaking and squawking on that thing on the job. He let me use it, you know. Someone sold me a planet for $20, a Henry Farney. I haven't heard the name, it's Paris. I haven't heard the name before or since. It was hot. That's how come you pick up that thing.
Oh, yeah?

Now, truthfully speaking, I could play two, three things on it. Didn't know what key was in, didn't even know the notes, just fingering it, you know. And I found out I could do that one, Valentine got me a chart. The fundamentals I had, see. All I had to do was go in the fingering, and I didn't need no clarinet, but the fiddle book was enough. I see. See, the clarinet went lower than the fiddle. Of course, it didn't go as high as the fiddle, but it went lower, you know. The C is the highest clarinet, I mean, highest note on the clarinet.
Did you ever play fiddle at the Dreamlands?
That's all I was playing. No, no. Southside? Yeah. Oh, sure.
Well, Ben Paul told me that you were the best fiddle player he ever had in his life.
Oh, goodness. Well, no, seriously, I was playing on a job at Dublin in a four-piece combination before I come out here, clarinet and fiddle. And just recently? Just before I come out here.
Uh-huh.

I got the fiddle here, but I was selling high-fi equipment in the daytime. I don't have time to practice. I never heard it there. Earl's been after me ever since I've been here to bring it in there. Why don't you? Uh-huh.
Get in shape. Play it, don't you?

Can't get in shape like that, no. Just play a few hours a day for a while. I said I'm so busy. That's the reason. Well, this is more important. What is? Get back on the fiddle. If I have to, I'll do it. I said, well, if I have to, I'll do it, but don't have to right now. I wish you would, though. Because I'd like to hear it. You know a good guitar playing time? No. Get a hold of the guitar and come on in my room. I'll play something for you. All right. I'm on the level.
I'll do that next time I'm in town.
I'm on the level. I got it here. You know, I didn't have it before last time.
I didn't have it like you used to ask you all the time.
Yeah. But I got it here. Girl called me up on the phone and had me playing Alvin Maria. It was a telephone. She couldn't think how it went. She was Alvin.
So how long did you stay with Alvin? I don't know.
About three, a little bit in three years, I guess. She couldn't remember.
She couldn't remember. Now, when is that, didn't you tell him once that he went to New York to record WBC Handy?
Tell me about that. What happened?
He came to Chicago, augmented his band. Remember Willie Tyler? You've heard of Willie Tyler, his violin player?
Willie Tyler?
Uh-huh. Very fine violinist. Myself, I was about five or six of us put in a band. Went to New York, made 33 sides for the Columbia people.
33 sides. How long did it take in the records?

Well, he said it would take two weeks, but we rehearsed on the train going to win. One half of that car, when we were in the, I don't remember what they called it, buffet car maybe. Yes. In those days. Yes. And we stayed in there and got permission after the thing closed and we practiced, you know. We made these records, but it was about five days. Straight five days.
What kind of tunes did you, I heard some of those.
All of his numbers, I guess. Yeah.
Big band, huh?
Yeah.
How many pieces in the band?

Well, 14, I guess, 15, something like that. Nelson, what's his name, Kincaid. They had two clarinets, King Phillips and Nelson Kincaid. I don't remember the other violin player Handy brought here with him. They had three fiddles in the band.
Two clarinets, three fiddles, and what kind of other instruments?
Well, Handy played cornet and trombone. Jasper Taylor on drums. You could only use the snares. And I don't remember whether they had a tube or not. That's a long time ago.
Where were the records made?
At the Columbia Steelers, New York. Don't ask the address, please. I don't know.
What kind of a studio was it?
Well, we played through megaphones.
How many megaphones were there?
How many what? How many megaphones did they have?
Three. Three. Everybody had to be picked up on three different megaphones, is that it?

And they stopped me two, three times. My boy kept hitting the megaphones. I'm not lying. The guy with two clarinet said, what's the matter? I said, what's the matter? He says, well, you hit it again. I'm trying to be clear back. He used to be some nice and plunk. Real loud, you know.
Could you play back a take in those days and hear what you were doing?
Oh, yeah. Yeah. They would play it back for you? Oh, yeah. Sure. That's the days when they said, now we'll make a good one. You know?
Uh-huh.
And you'd make three masters. Supposedly three masters. They'd select the best out of the three.
Oh, I see. You made everything three times.

Uh-huh. I see. Wax that thick. Yes. That thick. Oh. The amusing part about it, the ones that you'd make your test over, they had this razor blade adjustment with an electric fan. And it just shaved that impression off.
Lose it over again.
Yeah. Always. Just shaved it off real fine. I see. Those days of the killer, I'm telling you.
So then did you go right back to Chicago after you?

No. Went to work. Will Vaudry and, and, uh, a man, a other man. Dabney. You? Fort Dabney. Fort Dabney? Yeah, and Will Vaudry. They put me to work up there, at, uh, Ziegfield Roof. One hundred dollars a week. And I got homesick. I didn't mean to, I'm not.
You were just a kid at this time.
Yeah.
My God, you.
And I got, I got homesick, man. I couldn't stay there.
Weren't you scared in New York at that age?
Scared? Scared? Yeah. Why would I be scared? You were just a child. Well, why would I be scared? Scared? Some woman latch on to you. Ah. No. Well, nothing like that. Why would I be scared, man?
Well, you were in, in a, in a strange city.
I mean, the only thing that worried me, I got homesick. And, and, and on the way home, I went to, I went to work with Will May and Cook.
On the way home, what do you mean?
Yeah, I went to Philadelphia.
Oh, yeah?
I went to work with Will May and Cook. And he didn't pay off the band. Now, that was the experience.
Go ahead. Come in. She's on me.
Oh. In fact, you just leave it there.

So, so, Speedy Smith, a comedian, he said, by God, he says, how much do you owe you? I said, you know, me, I'm all in my money. He said, I'm going to get some of them. I said, don't worry about it. I think you'll get some money. He went in there. And I remember hearing him say, man, Cook, if you don't give me my money, I'm going to blow your damn brains out. Yeah. I get him. And I heard something like him putting a gun on. And I heard something like him putting a gun on. You know, he came out and gave me $16. I don't know how much he got, but I got $16. So, I went and stayed at a place called Mama Charleston where my mother and aunt used to stay in Philadelphia. She fed us, boarded, you know, slept. Mama Charleston says, well, says, I know your mama so well, says, I'm going to speak to a fellow. Says, I know you don't want to stay around Philadelphia. I'm going to speak to a fellow that works on, you know, one of his gangs on the road and see if I can get you a pass. Five dollars, she got me a pass for. I gave the man five dollars. And the pass didn't have a destination on it. He says, when you get on this train, says, you don't ask any questions. You know where you're going. Yeah. That's okay. Because if you have to ask questions, you have no business with the pass. I won't forget that. So, I get on this train. Get there to Pittsburgh. Track 10 is Chicago and track 12 is Wheeling, West Virginia. I guess on track 12. I know, ooh, that was awful. Ride all night. About 8 o'clock in the morning, the man says, Wheeling, West Virginia, far as we go. And that's the first time I knew I was going the wrong direction. Really? Oh, man, it was awful. And my trunk is in Chicago and I'm in Wheeling, West Virginia. All I got is my fiddle up in the, you know, bloody scare. Didn't have no birth. I don't know. Well, all I did was went to the telephone. I had about time I got through eating and carrying on, you know, odds and ends. I had a dollar, eating some hundred cents in my pocket to my name. Sent my mother telegram. Well, sure, I don't know no difference. I told her to send me a ticket. Quite nicely, she sent me just what I asked for. Sent me money for the ticket. Nothing extra. Nothing less. I'm down about 35 cents. I'm having a heck of a time. The train pulls out at 710 and the bag on telegram comes to 725. I got 35 cents to my name. So the baggage man that had been there that morning, he knew the predicament I was in. He comes to work that night and says, you still here? I says, I am. He says, well, I imagine you spend some money. I said, oh yeah, I got about 35 cents to my name. He said, are you sleepy? I said, no, not now. He said, when you do, he says, you get up on those trunks. He says, I got a sandwich. When I eat, I'll call you down. And sure enough, he did. Now, when I was with Earl Hines, I was 30. No, it wasn't with Earl Hines. It was Plantation Days, a show. We went to Pittsburgh. I tried to find that man. I wanted to reimburse him. Yes. That was pretty nice, you know. Sure. But he had retired. He didn't know where it was. That was 1923. Well, that was the hardest experience.
So finally you made it back to school?

I left that morning. That next morning. Going out, there was only two trains, you know, morning and evening. Oh, man, what an experience. You see, that caused me to, I don't care how good the job is or how well things look, I'm going to have my railroad fare return, regardless. My own person. I did that from now on. I don't care where I go. I'll be able to get back. Yeah. Sure. That's an awful experience. Now, you don't mind getting scared. Yeah, I got scared then.
Yes.

See, my mother, for some unknown reason, went downtown. I found out later. I saw her later getting the answers to the telegram. And just like women, she goes downtown, stay all day, nothing else to do. And she comes, she sees a telegram. I don't know what she said. It was 6.30 or so when she got the telegram, you know, finally opened the box. It was in the box. Of course, she sent the money. Too late for the train. Thank you.
John L. Howard, April 21st, 1957, Reel 2.
So what did you do when you came back to Chicago?
What did I do? Wait a minute. Oh, I went back to work with Elgar. And that's the same, that's the same...
Is he still playing in the same place?

Yes. He closed there and that's the band, that's when I went out on the road with Plantation Day and I come looking for this man. And that's the first time I went to Europe. Plantation Day, he went to Europe.
When is that?

1923. Oh, did you go to Europe in 23? Uh-huh. Come right back off the road and working with Carol Dixon and Jack Carter, says, boy, let's go to China. I said, man, no, I've just come back off of that thing. I don't want to move, you know. So he left. I was working at the Plantation with King Oliver. Something happened that got me disgusted and Jack's wife come in there and she says, anything you want me to tell Jack, I'm going to Shanghai. We're leaving in the morning, you know. I said, well, ask him if that offer is still good. He says, are you serious? I said, sure, I'm serious. He said, well, I'm going out and sending him a cable now. And sure enough, she got a cable from that answer before we close that morning. Right in the cafe. Bring all new music. No kidding. I'll never forget that. Oh, I was so happy. That was a wonderful trip to TKK, Toria Kisenkisen, Oriental Steamship Hotel System. Took me all the way around. I wish they'd had something like that now. Where did you play? Played all countries. Oriental Steamship Hotel System, like in Shanghai, was our headquarters for a while. The Dollar Line would come in on Monday, stay two days, leave around noon on Wednesday. The Canadian Pacific would come in that Wednesday morning, stay the Friday. The United States Lines would come in, President Harding, Monroe, you know, those different ones. And we were off Sunday. That's the same routine. We didn't play on the boats, but those are the boats. See, I left here and went on the Taiyo Maru. That's the Japanese boat. Went to Shanghai direct. But, see, I've been very fortunate. I've been to Moscow twice. Wilhelmina Hotel, went back and played at the National Hotel. When was that?
